what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: A laptop agent runs as me, so none do
sections.para: Operating systems have two hard walls, the kernel and the user account, and a laptop agent runs inside mine with all my credentials. So my agents run in Claude chat, Cowork in the cloud, Claude Code on the web and ChatGPT, with a vault as the shared drive. A dedicated machine is a separate question.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: No OS boundary separates local agents from my secrets
sections.para: Inside a user account, nothing the OS enforces stands between an agent and SSH keys, cloud credentials and browser sessions; desktop agents' sandboxes are settings. Fifteen months of incidents show the pattern. Four cloud surfaces each get only what their job needs, and a vault lets the laptop pass keys and nothing else.

sections.label: The question, and the short answer
sections.line: Local agents lack the isolation I would need
sections.para: I have no business need to run a model offline, and what a local agent would need, isolation better than online, no local agent offers. The models are fine; the place is the problem. On my laptop the grant is my whole account and the mandate is one document, which I would not accept from a contractor.

sections.label: The two walls
sections.line: Within one user account there is no third wall
sections.para: The OS separates the kernel and separates users, but a process I start runs with my rights. Desktop agents add approval prompts, allow lists and sandboxes, all enforced inside the wall marked me; Anthropic's docs say the default read scope includes ~/.ssh. A real boundary is a separate user, machine or cloud environment.

sections.label: The evidence
sections.line: Fifteen months of incidents show agents reaching account credentials
sections.para: From July 2025 to September 2026: deleted home directories and drives, pre-trust code execution in Claude Code and Cursor, CamoLeak exfiltration, tens of thousands of exposed OpenClaw instances and 341 malicious skills, a Cowork VM escape. GitGuardian counted 24,008 secrets in agent configs. Willison's lethal trifecta is present on every laptop by default.

sections.label: The setup
sections.line: Four cloud surfaces, each reaching only its job's needs
sections.para: Claude chat, with nothing connected and past-chat search off, is for thinking, while Cowork in the cloud does most agentic work with no repositories, only the vaults I hand it. Claude Code on the web gets one repository and a network allowlist. ChatGPT has no assets, only an occasional read key.

sections.label: The vault is the shared drive
sections.line: An encrypted vault lets isolated agents hand work over
sections.para: An sgit vault encrypts every file, name and message client-side, and each session gets a key out of band, pulls, works, commits and pushes. Cowork writes briefs that Claude Code pulls, so neither needs the other's reach. Only keys move between surfaces: a write key, a one-way read key and an append-only lane token.

sections.label: Same mandate, two deployments
sections.line: The cloud shrinks what an injected instruction can reach
sections.para: Moving to the cloud does not prevent prompt injection: a hidden instruction will be followed in either deployment. What changes is reach: one repository and one vault instead of my whole account. The barrier that holds is the small grant, not a cleverer filter, as Footprint and blast radius and The ultimate insider argue.

sections.label: What it costs me
sections.line: The trade-offs are real, cheap, and worth paying
sections.para: No agents without a connection, a key handed by hand each session, one vault per scope because Cowork lacks per-session secrets, no cross-chat memory, and two products with different flows. In return sessions start clean and a mistake costs a repository and vault with history: a bad afternoon, not an incident.

sections.label: Three things I wish the platforms gave me
sections.line: Agents need their own identity, secrets and key pair
sections.para: Each agent should have an account and name on its commits, secrets injected and revocable per agent, and a key pair to sign and receive encrypted messages. Claude Code on the web has the right shape for secrets; Cowork does not. Together they would let an agent run as itself rather than as me.

sections.label: The caveat, properly
sections.line: A dedicated, separate-account machine is a different model
sections.para: Everything here concerns a laptop holding the main account. A Mac mini or second laptop with separate Apple and Workspace accounts and nothing of mine resembles the cloud model, and vendor sandboxes would become a second layer. I have not run it yet, and will report when I have.

sections.label: What exists today, and what does not
sections.line: The setup runs; the three wishes do not exist
sections.para: Running today: the four surfaces, the vault as shared drive, per-session keys, a leak check before every commit, and the twelve-agent RiskMandate version. Missing: the three wishes as platform features, a desktop agent running as a separate OS user by default, and the dedicated-machine report.

sections.line: Sources: vendor docs, dated incident reports and earlier writing
sections.para: Sources include Anthropic's Claude Code sandboxing and Cowork documentation, incident reports from Gemini CLI and Amazon Q to Cowork SharedRoot and Muse, and GitGuardian's 2026 secrets reports. Also Simon Willison's lethal trifecta post and Dinis Cruz's June 2026 LinkedIn piece and 2025 MCP writing.
